pos: n. (a winged creature; in the law, a sacrificial victim in the cleansing rites; rendering Hebrew tsippor, Greek peteinon)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon brid, originally a young bird, a nestling. Scripture gives the smallest sacrificial animal one of its most beautiful ceremonies.
biblical_def: Bird is the poor man's offering and the leper's deliverance. The cleansing rite of Leviticus 14 requires “two birds alive and clean, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop” (Lev 14:4); one bird is killed “in an earthen vessel over running water” (Lev 14:5), and the living bird is dipped in its blood and let go into the open field. Two birds, one death, one release — the plainest picture of substitution in the ceremonial law, performed over a man the camp had cast out. The same rite cleanses a house (Lev 14:49). Birds appear too in the covenant of Genesis 15, where Abram divides the animals “but the birds divided he not” (Gen 15:10), and in Joseph's prison, where they eat from the baker's basket and then from the baker (Gen 40:17, 19). And the Lord Jesus measures His own homelessness by them: “the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head” (Mat 8:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bird properly as a chicken or the young of fowls, and hence a small fowl — noting that in modern use it is applied to all feathered flying animals.
webster_full: BIRD, n. Properly, a chicken, the young of fowls, and hence a small fowl.
In modern use, any fowl or flying animal covered with feathers.
A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.
BIRD, v.i. To catch birds; to take or seize birds.
scriptures: Lev 14:4
Then shall the priest command to take for him that is to be cleansed two birds alive and clean, and cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop:
Lev 14:5
And the priest shall command that one of the birds be killed in an earthen vessel over running water:
Mat 8:20
And Jesus saith unto him, The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.
And he took unto him all these, and divided them in the midst, and laid each piece one against another: but the birds divided he not.
corruption_summary: The ceremonial law read as arbitrary ritual rather than as gospel in pictures — so that a rite designed to show substitution and release is skipped as ancient hygiene.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The failure is neglect. Leviticus 14 is one of the most vivid gospel pictures in the Old Testament and is almost never preached. A man declared unclean, put outside the camp, and beyond human remedy is cleansed by two birds: one dies in an earthen vessel over running water, and the other, dipped in that blood, is released alive into the open field. Death and resurrection, substitution and liberty, performed over an outcast — and the entire cost is two small birds, within reach of the poorest man in Israel.

The principle to recover is that God's provision is scaled to the destitute. Birds are what the law prescribes when a lamb is beyond a family's means, which is why Mary and Joseph offered a pair of turtledoves at the Lord's presentation. And Matthew 8:20 turns the whole matter tender: the birds have nests, and the Son of man had nowhere to lay His head. He who provided the poor man's sacrifice was Himself poorer than the sacrifice.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsippor (H6833), a small bird, sparrow — from a root meaning to chirp; oph (H5775), winged creatures generally; Greek peteinon (G4071), a flying thing.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsippor (H6833) — a bird, sparrow; the two birds of the cleansing rite (Lev 14:4) and the sparrow alone upon the housetop (Psa 102:7).
Hebrew oph (H5775) — fowl, winged creatures; the collective term of the creation account and the food laws.
Greek strouthion (G4765) — a sparrow; two sold for a farthing, and not one forgotten before God (Luk 12:6).
usage: “Two birds alive and clean” — one dies, one is released; substitution in miniature.
“Killed in an earthen vessel over running water” — death and living water together.
“The birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head”.

pos: n. (the young of the herd; the idol of Sinai and of Bethel; rendering Hebrew egel, ben baqar, Greek moschos)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon cealf. In Scripture the calf is both the best thing a host can kill for a guest and the worst thing a nation ever made for itself.
biblical_def: Calf runs the full range from hospitality to apostasy. Abraham, entertaining three strangers, “ran unto the herd, and fetcht a calf tender and good” (Gen 18:7) — the costliest quick meal a herdsman could offer. Israel at Sinai takes the same animal and makes it a god: Aaron “fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf: and they said, These be thy gods, O Israel” (Exo 32:4). Note the exact form of the sin. They did not renounce the LORD or credit another deity with the exodus; they attributed His work to an image, and Aaron proclaimed a feast to the LORD the next day. It is a violation of the second commandment, not the first — the true God worshipped by a means He forbade. Moses grinds it to powder and makes them drink it (Exo 32:20), and the LORD plagues the people “because they made the calf, which Aaron made” (Exo 32:35) — a sentence that will not let the leader hide behind the crowd.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a calf as the young of the cow, and notes the golden calf of Scripture as an idol set up by the Israelites — also the calves of the lips, that is, praise.
webster_full: CALF, n. plu. calves. The young of the cow kind, or of the bovine genus of quadrupeds.
2. In contempt, an ignorant, stupid person; a dolt.
3. The thick fleshy part of the leg behind.
The golden calf, an idol set up by Aaron and the Israelites at Horeb.
scriptures: Exo 32:4

And he received them at their hand, and fashioned it with a graving tool, after he had made it a molten calf: and they said, These be thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt.
And the LORD plagued the people, because they made the calf, which Aaron made.
Gen 18:7
And Abraham ran unto the herd, and fetcht a calf tender and good, and gave it unto a young man; and he hasted to dress it.
And he took the calf which they had made, and burnt it in the fire, and ground it to powder, and strawed it upon the water, and made the children of Israel drink of it.
corruption_summary: Idolatry imagined as the worship of a rival god, when Exodus 32 shows the far commoner sin — the true God worshipped by means He never appointed, with His own name attached to it.
corruption_paragraphs: The golden calf is the definitive biblical case of will-worship, and its details are usually softened. Israel did not say here is a new god. They pointed at a calf and credited it with the exodus the LORD had performed, and Aaron announced “to morrow is a feast to the LORD” over it. The name was right; the means were invented; and the LORD sent a plague. That is why the regulative principle is not fussiness. Sincere worship of the true God through an unappointed medium is exactly what Sinai punished.

Exodus 32:35 deserves the last word in this entry, because of its strange doubled phrasing: the people were plagued because they made the calf, which Aaron made. The people made it and Aaron made it. Neither is permitted to hide behind the other — not the congregation behind the leader who gave them what they demanded, nor the leader behind the congregation that demanded it. Aaron's excuse in verse 24, that he threw in the gold and there came out this calf, is one of Scripture's most recognizable evasions.
roots_summary: Hebrew egel (H5695), a calf — the Sinai and Bethel idols; ben baqar, a son of the herd — Abraham's calf; Greek moschos (G3448), a calf — the fatted calf of Luke 15.
roots_lines: Hebrew egel (H5695) — a calf; the molten calf of Exo 32:4 and Jeroboam's two calves at Bethel and Dan (1Ki 12:28).
Hebrew ben baqar — a son of the herd; the tender and good calf Abraham killed for his guests (Gen 18:7).
Greek moschos (G3448) — a calf, young bull; the fatted calf killed for the returning prodigal (Luk 15:23).
usage: “These be thy gods, O Israel” — the LORD's work credited to an image.
“Because they made the calf, which Aaron made” — neither hides behind the other.
“A calf tender and good” — the same animal, offered rather than worshipped.

pos: n. (the pig; the standing biblical emblem of the unclean; rendering Hebrew chazir, Greek choiros)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon swin. In Scripture the swine is not merely unclean but the type of uncleanness, the animal by which apostasy is measured.
biblical_def: Swine is declared unclean by a precise test: “the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you” (Lev 11:7). The detail matters. The pig has the outward mark and lacks the inward process — the right feet, the wrong digestion — which makes it a natural emblem of the hypocrite. Deuteronomy adds that Israel must not even touch the carcase (Deu 14:8). By Isaiah's day, eating swine's flesh among the graves is the shorthand for a people gone entirely over to abomination (Isa 65:4), and Isaiah 66:3 sets swine's blood beside legitimate sacrifice to show that worship offered wrongly is not partial obedience but its opposite. Proverbs makes the sharpest single use: “As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion” (Pro 11:22). And the Lord Jesus forbids the casting of pearls before them (Mat 7:6) — a warning about wasting holy things on those who will only trample and turn.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines swine as a hog, a pachydermatous quadruped — noting that the word is used both as singular and plural, and that swine were unclean by the Mosaic law.
webster_full: SWINE, n. sing. and plu. A hog; a pachydermatous quadruped of the genus Sus.
The swine, though he divide the hoof, yet cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you. Lev. xi.
Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine. Matt. vii.
Swine's flesh was forbidden to the Israelites as an abomination.
scriptures: Lev 11:7
And the swine, though he divide the hoof, and be clovenfooted, yet he cheweth not the cud; he is unclean to you.
As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout, so is a fair woman which is without discretion.
Mat 7:6
Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you.
Isa 65:4
Which remain among the graves, and lodge in the monuments, which eat swine's flesh, and broth of abominable things is in their vessels;
corruption_summary: Discernment itself treated as the sin — any refusal to give holy things to those who trample them called judgmental — where Christ commands exactly that refusal.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 7:6 stands immediately after judge not, and the placement is deliberate: the same paragraph that forbids hypocritical condemnation commands a discriminating judgment about who receives what. Casting pearls before swine is forbidden, and obeying that requires deciding, about actual people, that they will trample and rend. A church that has been shamed out of all discernment cannot obey verse 6, and generally supposes it is being especially faithful to verse 1.

Leviticus 11:7 supplies the reason the pig became the emblem it is. The animal has the correct external mark — the divided hoof, visible to anyone — and lacks the internal one, the chewing of the cud, which no observer sees. That is the anatomy of hypocrisy exactly, and it is why Proverbs 11:22 lands so hard: a gold ring in a pig's snout is ornament attached to something that will take it straight back into the mud. Outward adornment cannot compensate for the missing inward work.
roots_summary: Hebrew chazir (H2386), swine, boar — the boar out of the wood that wastes the vine (Psa 80:13); Greek choiros (G5519), a young pig — the Gadarene herd and the prodigal's husks.
roots_lines: Hebrew chazir (H2386) — swine; unclean by the test of Lev 11:7, and the emblem of apostate feasting in Isa 65:4.
Greek choiros (G5519) — a swine; the herd into which the legion was sent (Mat 8:30), and the swine the prodigal was sent to feed (Luk 15:15).
Greek hus (G5300) — a sow; the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire (2Pe 2:22), nature unchanged by washing.
usage: “He cheweth not the cud; he is unclean” — the right feet, the wrong digestion.
“As a jewel of gold in a swine's snout” — ornament on something that returns to the mud.
“Neither cast ye your pearls before swine” — a command requiring discernment.

pos: n. (the scavenging animal of the ancient town; a term of contempt and of self-abasement; rendering Hebrew keleb, Greek kuon)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon docga. The biblical dog is not a pet but a half-wild scavenger of streets and battlefields, which governs every use of the word.
biblical_def: Dog in Scripture is almost always contemptuous, because the dog of the ancient town was a scavenger. Goliath takes it as an insult — “Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves?” (1Sa 17:43) — and David uses it of himself in self-abasement before Saul: “after a dead dog, after a flea” (1Sa 24:14). Mephibosheth uses the same phrase at the king's table: “What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?” (2Sa 9:8) — the sentence that makes David's kindness a picture of grace. The law files the dog with what is abominable, forbidding the price of a dog in the house of the LORD (Deu 23:18). And the most memorable use is the one that marks God's exactitude in judgment: dogs licked the blood of Naboth, and Elijah declares that in that place dogs shall lick Ahab's blood (1Ki 21:19) — a sentence carried out to the letter in 1 Kings 22:38.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the dog as a species of quadruped of the genus Canis, and notes its Scriptural use as a term of reproach for what is impudent, mean or contemptible.
webster_full: DOG, n. A species of quadrupeds, belonging to the genus Canis, of many varieties.
2. It is used for male, when applied to several other animals; as a dog fox.
3. An appellation of contempt or reproach.
Without are dogs, and sorcerers, and whoremongers. Rev. xxii.
scriptures: And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, Hast thou killed, and also taken possession? And thou shalt speak unto him, saying, Thus saith the LORD, In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine.
And he bowed himself, and said, What is thy servant, that thou shouldest look upon such a dead dog as I am?
And the Philistine said unto David, Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves? And the Philistine cursed David by his gods.
Thou shalt not bring the hire of a whore, or the price of a dog, into the house of the LORD thy God for any vow: for even both these are abomination unto the LORD thy God.
corruption_summary: Judgment imagined as vague and general, where Scripture makes it geographically precise — in the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth — and mercy imagined as owed, where the dead dog knows it is not.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The two neglected doctrines are precision in judgment and astonishment at mercy. Elijah's word to Ahab names a location: in the place where dogs licked Naboth's blood, dogs shall lick thine. Ahab repented partially, judgment was delayed, and 1 Kings 22:38 records it landing exactly — the chariot washed in the pool of Samaria, the dogs licking his blood. God's justice is not approximate.

The principle to recover on the other side is Mephibosheth's. Summoned to the king's table, lame in both feet, the grandson of the house David had every political reason to destroy, he says: such a dead dog as I am. That is not false modesty; it is an accurate reading of his position. And he eats at the king's table continually. A believer who has stopped being surprised by that has begun to think of grace as a wage, and the word dog in Scripture exists partly to prevent it.
roots_summary: Hebrew keleb (H3611), a dog — also the root of the name Caleb; Greek kuon (G2965), a dog; kunarion (G2952), a little dog or house-dog — the word in the Syrophenician woman's exchange.
roots_lines: Hebrew keleb (H3611) — a dog, scavenger; used in contempt (1Sa 17:43) and in self-abasement (2Sa 9:8).
Greek kuon (G2965) — a dog; Paul's beware of dogs (Php 3:2), and the dogs left outside the city (Rev 22:15).
Greek kunarion (G2952) — a little dog, one kept in the house; the diminutive the Syrophenician woman seized upon to claim the crumbs (Mar 7:28).
usage: “In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth” — judgment named to the location.
“Such a dead dog as I am” — and he ate at the king's table continually.
“Am I a dog, that thou comest to me with staves?” — the giant's idea of an insult.

pos: n. (a seed-bearing plant; the original food of man and beast; rendering Hebrew eseb, yaraq, Greek lachanon)
etymology: From Latin herba, grass, green growth. In Genesis the herb is a category of creation, defined by a single property: it bears seed.
biblical_def: Herb is a creation category before it is a kitchen one, and its defining mark is reproduction: “Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself” (Gen 1:11). Two things are established there and never revoked: creatures reproduce after their kind, and the herb carries its own future inside it. God then assigns it as food — “I have given you every herb bearing seed… to you it shall be for meat” (Gen 1:29) — and to the beasts as well, “every green herb for meat” (Gen 1:30). The original diet of man and animal alike is vegetable, and flesh is granted only after the flood: “even as the green herb have I given you all things” (Gen 9:3). Between the two stands the curse, which puts labour into the arrangement: “Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field” (Gen 3:18).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an herb as a plant or vegetable with a soft or succulent stalk or stem, which dies to the root every year — distinguished from a tree or shrub by its perishing stem.
webster_full: HERB, n. erb. A plant or vegetable with a soft or succulent stalk or stem, which dies to the root every year, and is thus distinguished from a tree and a shrub.
2. In the Linnean botany, that part of a vegetable which springs from the root and is terminated by the fructification.
3. Grass; herbage.
God said, let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed. Gen. i.
scriptures: Gen 1:11
And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so.
Gen 1:29

And God said, Behold, I have given you every herb bearing seed, which is upon the face of all the earth, and every tree, in the which is the fruit of a tree yielding seed; to you it shall be for meat.
Gen 9:3
Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you; even as the green herb have I given you all things.
Gen 3:18
Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee; and thou shalt eat the herb of the field;
corruption_summary: After his kind quietly abandoned, and the herb's self-contained seed treated as an accident — while diet is moralized into a religion with clean and unclean of its own devising.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 1:11 says twice what modern origins accounts deny: things reproduce after their kind, and the seed is in itself. The dictionary holds the six-day creation of Genesis as its standard, and it holds it here at the level of the herb, because the phrase is repeated at every stage of the account rather than mentioned once. Whatever variation occurs within kinds — and it plainly occurs — the text asserts fixed kinds each carrying its own seed, and the assertion is structural to the chapter.

The second drift is dietary moralism. Genesis grants the herb, then grants flesh after the flood, and the New Testament forecloses the argument entirely: the kingdom of God is not meat and drink, and he that eateth is not to despise him that eateth not. Where eating becomes a system of purity and defilement of a person's own devising, Romans 14 is being violated in both directions — and Paul, notably, calls the man who eateth herbs the weaker brother, and then commands the stronger not to despise him.
roots_summary: Hebrew eseb (H6212), herb, green plant — the seed-bearing category of Gen 1:11; yaraq (H3419), green things, garden herbs; Greek lachanon (G3001), a garden herb, potherb.
roots_lines: Hebrew eseb (H6212) — herb, herbage; the seed-yielding creation category and the food of Gen 1:29-30.
Hebrew yaraq (H3419) — green, herbs; better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith (Pro 15:17).
Greek lachanon (G3001) — a garden herb; the mustard seed becoming the greatest among herbs (Mat 13:32).
usage: “The herb yielding seed… whose seed is in itself” — each kind carries its own future.
“I have given you every herb bearing seed… for meat” — the original diet.
“Thou shalt eat the herb of the field” — the same food, now with thorns in the way.

pos: n. (the blossom of a plant; in the tabernacle, the ornament of the candlestick; rendering Hebrew perach, tsits, Greek anthos)
etymology: From Latin flos, a blossom. Scripture uses the flower for two opposite things: the beaten gold that never fades, and the flesh that fades by noon.
biblical_def: Flower serves two purposes in Scripture, and the contrast is the doctrine. In the tabernacle it is gold: the candlestick is beaten work, “his shaft, and his branches, his bowls, his knops, and his flowers, shall be of the same” (Exo 25:31), with almond blossoms worked into every branch (Exo 25:33) — flowers that will never wilt, in the one room lit day and night. Everywhere else the flower is the emblem of what does not last: “As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15); “All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field” (Isa 40:6). Peter quotes it and adds the contrast that gives the figure its point — the flower falls away, “but the word of the Lord endureth for ever” — and James applies it specifically to the rich man, who “shall fade away in his ways” (Jas 1:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a flower as the blossom of a plant, the part which contains the organs of fructification — and figuratively the prime, the best part, or that which is most beautiful and least lasting.
webster_full: FLOWER, n. In botany, that part of a plant which contains the organs of fructification, with their coverings.
2. The early part of life, or rather of manhood; the prime; youthful vigor; youth; as, the flower of age or of life.
3. The best or finest part of a thing; the most valuable part.
4. That which is most distinguished for any thing valuable.
scriptures: Isa 40:6
The voice said, Cry. And he said, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all the goodliness thereof is as the flower of the field:
As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth.
Jas 1:11

For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways.
And thou shalt make a candlestick of pure gold: of beaten work shall the candlestick be made: his shaft, and his branches, his bowls, his knops, and his flowers, shall be of the same.
corruption_summary: A culture organized around the postponement of fading — youth extended, decline denied — which makes Isaiah 40:6 unbearable and therefore unread.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 40:6 is not a mood; it is a commissioned message. The voice says Cry, and the prophet asks what he shall cry, and the answer is: all flesh is grass. That is what God appointed to be proclaimed at the opening of the greatest comfort chapter in the prophets. An age that spends its resources denying exactly this — extending youth, editing images, deferring every reminder of decline — has not found a way around the verse; it has only made itself unable to hear the comfort that follows it.

The candlestick is the counterweight, and it is worth setting the two together. In the holy place stood a lampstand of beaten gold covered in almond flowers, blossoming permanently in a room with no window, lit continually. Israel's flowers of gold never faded, and they were the light the priests worked by. So Scripture does not merely tell a fading man that he fades; it shows him gold flowers in the sanctuary and tells him the word of the Lord endureth for ever. The fading is real and it is not the last word.
roots_summary: Hebrew perach (H6525), a blossom, bud — the candlestick's flowers; tsits (H6731), a flower, and also the golden plate on the high priest's mitre; Greek anthos (G438), a blossom.
roots_lines: Hebrew perach (H6525) — a bud, blossom; the beaten-gold flowers of the candlestick (Exo 25:31) and the blossoming of Aaron's rod.
Hebrew tsits (H6731) — a flower, and the golden plate of the mitre; the fading flower of the field (Isa 40:6).
Greek anthos (G438) — a flower; Peter and James both quote Isaiah's figure against human glory (1Pe 1:24; Jas 1:11).
usage: “All flesh is grass… as the flower of the field” — the commissioned message.
“His bowls, his knops, and his flowers, shall be of the same” — gold flowers that never fade.
“The flower thereof falleth… so also shall the rich man fade away”.

pos: n. (deep mud; the emblem of a place with no footing; rendering Hebrew tit, yaven)
etymology: From Old Norse myrr, a bog. Scripture's interest in mire is not that it is dirty but that it offers no standing — a man in it cannot get purchase.
biblical_def: Mire is deep mud, and its terror in Scripture is the absence of a floor. The psalmist's cry is exact: “I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing” (Psa 69:2), and the prayer follows, “Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink” (Psa 69:14) — a psalm the New Testament applies repeatedly to Christ. Jeremiah lives the figure literally: lowered by cords into a dungeon where “there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire” (Jer 38:6) — the prophet of God at the bottom of a cistern for telling the truth. Job says God has cast him into it (Job 30:19). And Isaiah gives the diagnosis that turns the image inward: “the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt” (Isa 57:20) — the mire is not only what a man sinks into but what an unquiet heart throws up.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mire as deep mud, earth so wet as to be soft and adhesive — and as a verb, to plunge or fix in mire, to set fast in mud.
webster_full: MIRE, n. Deep mud; earth so wet and soft as to yield to the feet and to wheels.
MIRE, v.t. To plunge and fix in mire; to set or stall in mud.
2. To soil or daub with mud or foul matter.
MIRE, v.i. To sink in mud, or to sink so deep as to be unable to move forward.
scriptures: Psa 69:2
I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing: I am come into deep waters, where the floods overflow me.
Jer 38:6

Then took they Jeremiah, and cast him into the dungeon of Malchiah the son of Hammelech, that was in the court of the prison: and they let down Jeremiah with cords. And in the dungeon there was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire.
But the wicked are like the troubled sea, when it cannot rest, whose waters cast up mire and dirt.
Deliver me out of the mire, and let me not sink: let me be delivered from them that hate me, and out of the deep waters.
corruption_summary: Restlessness sold as ambition and treated as a virtue, where Isaiah names it the mark of the wicked — a sea that cannot rest, casting up mire and dirt.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 57:20 diagnoses a condition the age admires. The troubled sea cannot rest, and what it produces is mire and dirt — the churning itself is the problem, and the filth is a by-product of the restlessness. A culture that measures a life by its striving, and that cannot tolerate stillness for the length of a meal, has made a virtue of exactly what the prophet names as the estate of the wicked. And the verse ends with the sentence that explains it: there is no peace, saith my God, to the wicked.

The pastoral half is Psalm 69, and it is the psalm of the Man of Sorrows. I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing. Whatever a believer means by that sentence, Christ meant it first and more deeply, which is why the psalm can be prayed honestly by anyone in it. Jeremiah's cistern makes the same point historically: the man in the mire was not being punished for unfaithfulness but suffering for it, and the man who drew him out did it with old rags and cords, one act of ordinary kindness in a collapsing city.
roots_summary: Hebrew tit (H2916), mud, clay, mire; yaven (H3121), deep mire, the sinking kind — used in Psa 69:2; bots (H1206), mire, marsh.
roots_lines: Hebrew tit (H2916) — mud, mire, clay; trodden like the mire of the streets (Isa 10:6) and cast up by the troubled sea (Isa 57:20).
Hebrew yaven (H3121) — deep, sinking mire; used only twice, both in the Psalms, both of a man with no footing (Psa 40:2; Psa 69:2).
Hebrew bor (H953) — a pit, cistern; Jeremiah's dungeon with no water but mire (Jer 38:6), and the pit from which Psa 40:2 lifts a man to a rock.
usage: “I sink in deep mire, where there is no standing” — the terror is the missing floor.
“There was no water, but mire: so Jeremiah sunk in the mire” — the prophet at the bottom.
“The wicked are like the troubled sea… whose waters cast up mire and dirt”.

pos: n. (an island or coastland; in the prophets, the far nations awaiting the Messiah; rendering Hebrew i, plural iyyim)
etymology: From Latin insula through Old French. The Hebrew i means a coastland or habitable shore, and in Isaiah it becomes shorthand for the ends of the earth.
biblical_def: Isle in the Authorized Version usually means a coastland, and in the prophets it is a missionary word. The table of nations begins it: “By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue” (Gen 10:5) — the nations scattered at Babel, filed under the isles. Isaiah then makes them the object of the Servant's work: “He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law” (Isa 42:4) — a promise quoted over Christ in Matthew 12, and one that no reading confined to Israel can contain. The Psalter joins the summons: “The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof” (Psa 97:1). And Isaiah 24:15 calls for His name to be glorified “in the isles of the sea”. To the Hebrew ear the isles were the outermost places, past the last trade route — and they are precisely where the prophets expect the gospel to arrive.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an isle as a tract of land surrounded by water, or a detached portion of land embosomed in the ocean — noting that in Scripture it often denotes a maritime country or coast.
webster_full: ISLE, n. ile. A tract of land surrounded by water; an island.
In Scripture, isle sometimes denotes a country not connected with any known continent, or one distant from Judea.
The isles shall wait for his law. Is. xlii.
2. A passage in a church or cathedral; more properly aisle.
scriptures: Isa 42:4
He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law.
Gen 10:5
By these were the isles of the Gentiles divided in their lands; every one after his tongue, after their families, in their nations.
Psa 97:1
The LORD reigneth; let the earth rejoice; let the multitude of isles be glad thereof.
Wherefore glorify ye the LORD in the fires, even the name of the LORD God of Israel in the isles of the sea.
corruption_summary: The Great Commission narrowed to what is near and comfortable, while the prophets set the Servant's reach at the isles — the last places on the map, waiting for His law.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The failure is one of horizon. Isaiah 42:4 does not present the isles as an optional extension of the Servant's work but as its measure: He will not fail nor be discouraged till He has set judgment in the earth, and the isles wait for His law. A church whose vision ends at its own coastline has a smaller Christ than Isaiah's, and the correction is not guilt but expectation. The isles are waiting; the outcome is not in doubt.

Genesis 10:5 supplies the historical frame that makes the promise sweet. The isles of the Gentiles are the scattering of Babel, divided by tongue and family and nation — humanity fragmented under judgment. Isaiah's promise gathers those same coastlands back under one law, and Pentecost reverses the tongues. The last places on the ancient map are exactly where the Servant's dominion is said to reach, which is why the missionary movement was reading these texts rightly.
roots_summary: Hebrew i (H339), a habitable coastland, island — plural iyyim, the isles of the prophets; the word marks the outermost inhabited edge of the known world.
roots_lines: Hebrew i (H339) — coastland, island, region across the sea; the isles of the Gentiles (Gen 10:5) and the isles that wait for His law (Isa 42:4).
Hebrew iyyim — the plural; in Isaiah it functions as a synonym for the ends of the earth (Isa 41:5; Isa 49:1).
Greek nesos (G3520) — an island; the Septuagint's rendering, and the word for Patmos where the Revelation was given (Rev 1:9).
usage: “The isles shall wait for his law” — the Servant's reach measured at the map's edge.
“The isles of the Gentiles divided… every one after his tongue” — Babel's scattering.
“Let the multitude of isles be glad thereof” — the far coasts summoned to rejoice.

pos: n. and v. (the sound following lightning; the voice of God in judgment; rendering Hebrew ra'am, qol, Greek bronte)
etymology: From Anglo-Saxon thunor. The Hebrew for thunder is often simply qol, voice — so that to an Israelite ear thunder was not merely a noise but speech.
biblical_def: Thunder is the sound of God speaking in Scripture, and it is used to make men know who owns the earth. The seventh plague is announced with it: “the LORD sent thunder and hail, and the fire ran along upon the ground” (Exo 9:23), and Moses tells Pharaoh the thunder will cease “that thou mayest know how that the earth is the LORD'S” (Exo 9:29) — the point of the miracle is stated as ownership. At Sinai the thunders accompany the giving of the law, and the whole camp trembles (Exo 19:16); when the people see them they stand afar off (Exo 20:18), which is the right instinct in the wrong direction. Hannah's song puts thunder in the future tense of judgment: “out of heaven shall he thunder upon them: the LORD shall judge the ends of the earth” (1Sa 2:10). And the Lord Jesus names two disciples Boanerges, the sons of thunder — a temperament He does not remove but harnesses, since one of them wrote the epistles of love.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines thunder as the sound which follows an explosion of electricity in the atmosphere — and figuratively, any loud noise, or a denunciation uttered with authority.
webster_full: THUN´DER, n. The sound which follows an explosion of electricity or lightning; the report of a discharge of electrical fluid.
2. Thunder is used for lightning, or for a thunder-bolt, either originally through ignorance, or by ellipsis.
3. Any loud noise; as the thunder of cannon.
4. Denunciation published; as the thunders of the Vatican.
scriptures: Exo 9:29

And Moses said unto him, As soon as I am gone out of the city, I will spread abroad my hands unto the LORD; and the thunder shall cease, neither shall there be any more hail; that thou mayest know how that the earth is the LORD'S.

And it came to pass on the third day in the morning, that there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud; so that all the people that was in the camp trembled.

The adversaries of the LORD shall be broken to pieces; out of heaven shall he thunder upon them: the LORD shall judge the ends of the earth; and he shall give strength unto his king, and exalt the horn of his anointed.
And all the people saw the thunderings, and the lightnings, and the noise of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking: and when the people saw it, they removed, and stood afar off.
corruption_summary: Nature emptied of its Owner — weather as mere mechanism — and a God so tamed that nothing about Him could make a camp tremble.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 9:29 states the purpose of the thunder without ambiguity: that thou mayest know how that the earth is the LORD'S. Not that the atmosphere behaves in certain ways, and not that Pharaoh should be frightened generally, but that ownership should be established. The modern habit of explaining a mechanism and considering the matter closed does not contradict this; it simply changes the subject. Scripture never disputes secondary causes and never allows them to be the whole account.

The related loss is the fear of God. At Sinai the people saw the thunderings and removed, and stood afar off — and Moses tells them not to fear, because God is come to prove them, that His fear may be before their faces. That is not a contradiction but the whole doctrine in one place: the terror that drives a man away is to be replaced by the reverence that keeps him from sinning. Where nothing about God could possibly make a congregation tremble, something has been lost that Sinai considered basic.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'am (H7482), thunder, a roar; qol (H6963), voice, sound — regularly rendered thunder; Greek bronte (G1027), thunder — in Boanerges, sons of thunder.
roots_lines: Hebrew qol (H6963) — voice, sound; the plural qolot is the word for the thunders of Sinai (Exo 19:16), so thunder is literally voices.
Hebrew ra'am (H7482) — to thunder, roar; Hannah's out of heaven shall he thunder upon them (1Sa 2:10).
Greek bronte (G1027) — thunder; the surname given to James and John (Mar 3:17), and the voice like thunder in Revelation (Rev 14:2).
usage: “That thou mayest know how that the earth is the LORD'S” — the purpose of the thunder stated.
“All the people that was in the camp trembled” — the right instinct at Sinai.
“The sons of thunder” — a temperament harnessed rather than removed.

pos: n. (a shaking of the earth; rendering Hebrew ra'ash, Greek seismos)
etymology: A plain English compound. The Greek seismos gives us seismic, and is also the word for the storm on the Sea of Galilee — a shaking, whether of land or water.
biblical_def: Earthquake in Scripture is both a real historical event and a sign, and the Bible is careful not to confuse the two. Amos dates his prophecy by one: “two years before the earthquake” in the days of Uzziah (Amo 1:1), and Zechariah still remembers people fleeing from it centuries later (Zec 14:5) — ordinary chronology, anchored to a disaster everybody recalled. The great lesson comes at Horeb, where Elijah, exhausted and suicidal, is given wind, earthquake, and fire in succession, and told of each: “the LORD was not in the earthquake” (1Ki 19:11) — and then comes “a still small voice” (1Ki 19:12). God is not absent from the spectacular; He is simply not confined to it, and the prophet who wanted fire from heaven is answered by a whisper. The two earthquakes that matter most in the canon are at the cross, where one convinces a centurion (Mat 27:54), and at the tomb, where the angel rolls back the stone (Mat 28:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an earthquake as a shaking, trembling or concussion of the earth, sometimes a slight tremor, at other times a violent shock which overturns buildings and swallows up cities.
webster_full: EARTH´QUAKE, n. A shaking, trembling or concussion of the earth; sometimes a slight tremor; at other times a violent shaking or convulsion.
Earthquakes are usually preceded by a rumbling noise, and often accompanied by an eruption of fire, water or vapor.
There shall be famines and pestilences and earthquakes in divers places. Matt. xxiv.
The whole tract of country is subject to earthquakes.
scriptures: And he said, Go forth, and stand upon the mount before the LORD. And, behold, the LORD passed by, and a great and strong wind rent the mountains, and brake in pieces the rocks before the LORD; but the LORD was not in the wind: and after the wind an earthquake; but the LORD was not in the earthquake:
And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice.
Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching Jesus, saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly, saying, Truly this was the Son of God.
Amo 1:1

The words of Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.
corruption_summary: Disaster mined for prophetic significance on one side and drained of all meaning on the other — while Matthew 24:7 lists earthquakes precisely among the things that are not the end.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation produces readers who tally earthquakes as proof that the end has arrived. The Lord Jesus anticipated the impulse and forestalled it: famines, pestilences, and earthquakes in divers places are named, and the sentence just before says the end is not yet. These are the birth pangs of the whole age, not a countdown. The opposite error treats them as pure geology with no message at all, which the centurion at the cross would not have recognized — he saw the earthquake and said, Truly this was the Son of God.

1 Kings 19 is the passage to sit with, because it addresses a servant of God at the end of his strength. Elijah had just called down fire and won, and he is under a juniper tree wanting to die. God gives him wind, earthquake, and fire — the whole vocabulary of Sinai — and says He is in none of them, then speaks in a still small voice. The ministry that follows is not spectacular: anoint two kings and a successor, and know that seven thousand have not bowed. God is not in the earthquake, and He is not finished with the man who needed one and got a whisper.
roots_summary: Hebrew ra'ash (H7494), a quaking, shaking, commotion; Greek seismos (G4578), a shaking — used both of the earthquake at the tomb and of the tempest on the sea (Mat 8:24).
roots_lines: Hebrew ra'ash (H7494) — a quaking, rushing; the earthquake in the days of Uzziah (Amo 1:1; Zec 14:5).
Greek seismos (G4578) — a shaking, tempest, earthquake; the same word for the storm the Lord stilled (Mat 8:24) and the quake at His resurrection (Mat 28:2).
Hebrew qol demamah daqqah — a still small voice, literally a sound of thin silence; what came after the earthquake at Horeb (1Ki 19:12).
usage: “The LORD was not in the earthquake” — not absent from the spectacular, but not confined to it.
“Two years before the earthquake” — ordinary chronology anchored to a real disaster.
“Saw the earthquake… Truly this was the Son of God” — a centurion reads the sign.
